text: Lesson 18 fixed individual predicates. This lesson steps back further, to the shape of the whole operation: row by row, or the whole set at once. That choice usually matters more than any single predicate rewrite.

A cursor iterates a result set one row at a time — the same mental model as a loop in a general-purpose language. Every iteration is a separate statement execution with its own overhead: a plan lookup, a log entry, lock acquisition. For ten rows nobody notices. For a hundred thousand, that overhead compounds into minutes.

The same update, expressed as a single set operation. SQL Server evaluates it once, builds one plan, and processes every matching row in one coordinated pass — no per-row loop, no repeated round trips.

This isn't a minor detail — it's the model the entire relational engine was built around. Every technique from earlier in this course, index seeks, covering indexes, execution plans, assumes set-based operations as the unit of work being optimized. Cursors still have a place, but only when the per-row logic is genuinely sequential and can't be expressed as a set operation.
Set-based thinking is the default for a reason. Next up: avoiding common anti-patterns — implicit conversions, NOLOCK misuse, and scalar UDFs in WHERE clauses.
